options.label: We'll help.
options.tooltip: Leave it to us: whatever has gone wrong, we'll put it right before dusk.

nodes.text: Good morning, Kelderby! And good morning, new faces: welcome to Kelderby! Today is the festival: a feast on the square, the bell at dusk, the lighthouse lamp over the bay and the castle's fireworks at midnight. Nothing can possibly go wrong.

That? That is everything going wrong at once. The boatwright's cargo boat has turned over in the bay with the feast in it. The cooper's goats are up the terraces. The bell rope has snapped. And the lighthouse lamp went out in the night, and the keeper is up there swearing at it. Pick one. Pick all of them. Be back on this stage by dusk.
How is it going? Don't tell me. Tell me at dusk. Smile at the town.

options.label: We're ready. Let them come.
options.tooltip: There is no going back: the raid begins at once, and the rest of the town waits until it is over.

nodes.text: You're back! Is it all put right, the lamp and the bell, the goats, the crates, the fireworks? Then look out past the lighthouse, darlings, because I have been looking all afternoon. Striped sails. That is Captain Gull, who comes every year he hears we have a cake worth taking, and this year he has brought friends: big ones. When his horn blows there is no more running about the town: it is this stage, the main street and the cake until it is over. So get ready first. Torvald sells good iron at his counter, and whatever else the town has given you today, bring it.

options.label: Begin.
options.tooltip: Open the festival, whatever the day has made of it.

nodes.text: Look at them. Look at all of them. Right. Whatever happened today, that is the festival now. Shall I begin?

Oskar's pig race, whenever you dare it: round the whole town on his racing pigs, one rider to a pig, and through the cathedral on the way. Ask him at the bakery's door. And the fair field behind the beach has its stalls out, and every one of them is giving something away. And they do say the big grey cat by the duck pond talks, if it likes you.

options.label: We're going up.
options.tooltip: Climb the tower and light the lamp.

nodes.text: Went out at three this morning. Wick's fine, oil's fine, the lamp is sulking. Also the stairs gave way in three places on the way up, so you'll be jumping. Light it for me and I'll owe you.

A fox. In MY storeroom. With MY key. And now it is off up the road with it, and the fireworks are locked in until somebody catches it. I would go myself, but I do not go up to the castle any more. Not since the garrison started getting up again.

So the fox has been seen. When you have the key, mind the castle: the old garrison gets up in the yard when it is quiet, and they do not know they are dead. The fireworks are in the cellar under the great hall, behind the old grate, and the grate lifts only for the four watch fires in the yard, lit in the proper order. I wrote the order down and left the note in my chest by the well. Light one out of turn and the lot go out.
Ghost stories. Lady Agathe's family say there is a treasure of the old lords somewhere in it. Forty years I have swept that castle, and if there is, it is better hidden than my storeroom key.
The cake is done. Four tiers, candied cherries, a sugar lighthouse on top. It goes on the stage at dusk and nobody breathes on it until midnight.

options.label: We'll race.
options.tooltip: Oskar's cart takes the whole party down to the start line, wherever each of you is, and the race is on: the rest of the day waits until it has been run.

nodes.text: My racing pigs! Saddled since dawn and eating their heads off. Round the whole town: up through the woods behind the farms, through the cathedral garden and the churchyard, in at the cathedral's side door and out at its great front door, down the main street and home along the lower lane to the meadow track. Every checkpoint on the way, in order, or it does not count. A carter called Ulla has won it three years running and will not stop saying so. Race her?

My counter sells bread and pie for the town's pennies, even today. And if it is honey you want, the bee meadow behind the beach: the hives are full, and there are bottles in the honey stand for whoever fills them. The lookout up the castle road has the best view in Kelderby; people leave things up there.
My dear, I have watched sixty-one of these festivals and every one of them nearly did not happen. Go on. I shall be in the front row tonight.

Older. My husband's family swore the old lords hid their finest arms somewhere in it before the last siege, and never came back for them. Forty years I lived up there, and found nothing but draughts and a garrison that would not lie down, so I came down to the town. Perhaps it is true. Nobody knows how one would get at it, if it were.

If the hills are too much for your legs, Runa at the inn's stable hires out her grey mare. And Torvald the smith sells good iron at his counter on the main street, for the pennies the town is handing out. When I was a girl there was a cave up the island's seaward flank, past the end of the path under the hill, all green and glowing. I expect it is still there.

options.label: We'll row out.
options.tooltip: Take Sverre's boat out into the bay and bring the crates in.

nodes.text: Turned her over on the bar, didn't I. Six crates of the feast are bobbing about out on the shoals, past the deep water, and two of them out past the outer bar; go round by the channel at the harbour end of it. Take the Herring, the boat by the steps; she rows true. They won't stay afloat long once the tide's on them.
Mind the bar. The boats don't, which is how we got here.

The games yard above the harbour house has prizes in its stalls, and the archery butts out along the track from the quay's far end keep a sheaf of arrows for anyone with a bow. The gulls out on the beacon point are generous, if they like the look of you. So is the hen at the croft.

options.label: We'll bring them home.
options.tooltip: Fetch wheat from the field and lead the three goats back into this pen.

nodes.text: My three goats are out of the pen. Pearl, the youngest of my nannies, has gone up onto the terraces behind the fishmonger's, into the orchard above the track. Barley, the best milker in Kelderby, is at the wayside spring, a little way up the castle road. And the Admiral, the old billy who undid the latch, is in the orchard out on the farm track. Each of them has a name over its head, and they'll all follow wheat anywhere. The field's out on the farm track.

Hold the wheat up where they can see it and walk slowly. This pen, mind, on the main street: not the sheep's, not the cows'. Once a goat is in here it stays put, so bring them one at a time if you like. When all three are in, drop the latch on the gate.

Pearl is in the orchard on the terraces: down the main street to the fishmonger's, through its back yard onto the terrace track, and along it to the orchard above. Barley is at the wayside spring, the first stop up the castle road from the square. And the Admiral is in the orchard out on the farm track: along lane 5 beside this pen and out past the pond.

And one more thing. Runa's grey mare? Runa will not lend her without pennies. But if you want her without paying, tell Runa her sister's cow is calving. She would leave a burning stable for that cow. You did not hear it from me.
All three home and the latch down. Pearl, Barley, the Admiral. I have told them all about you.
I have penned the two that are left. I am not going to talk about the other one today.
I fetched them myself in the end. They are waiting somewhere you will see tonight, and I am not saying where.
If you see a goat anywhere it shouldn't be, it's one of mine.

options.label: Give me the bow.
options.tooltip: Take Vidar's bow and arrows and shoot the target in the bell tower.

nodes.text: By-law fourteen: the bell rings at dusk. The rope snapped this morning, and the knot is caught on the archery target up in the tower's opening, where nobody can reach it. I have a bow. I have never once hit anything with it. Three clean hits would shake the knot free.

By-law nine: the herb stall in the cathedral's garden feeds whoever is hungry. By-law twelve: on festival day, and on no other, a pig may be ridden through the cathedral, in at the side door and out at the front, if it is racing. Ask Oskar. The by-laws are very clear on pigs. By-law three: no feeding the cat by the duck pond. Nobody has ever obeyed by-law three. The cat has seen to that.

happening.subject: npc/runa
happening.text: Runa believes her sister's cow is calving, and reaches for her coat.

options.label: Your sister's cow is calving!
options.tooltip: Kettil's tip: send Runa off up the farm track to her sister's calving cow, and take the mare while she is gone.

nodes.text: Moss is in the back stable. She can be hired, at the barrel there, for pennies, which the town is handing out today to anyone who mends something. She is not for running down the main street with.
Forge is cold. Holiday. The counter by the door sells what I made this winter, for the town's pennies. And in the back stands an iron man I have been building since the snow.

Iron, all of him, except the head. An iron man's head is a carved pumpkin, face and all, and every pumpkin in Kelderby was cut into a lantern this morning; the scarecrows will not give theirs up, so do not ask them. Put one on the anvil there once the feast's crates are landed, and he will see. The lantern cutters had a barrel of them out at the allotments, past the far end of the quay.

options.label: Wake him (5 pennies).
options.tooltip: Show Torvald 5 pennies, and his iron man walks down to the square at dusk and fights beside you. Torvald will not take the job for less than 5 pennies in the party's purse.

nodes.text: He has his head. He can see. Waking him is the dear part: 5 pennies to me, and he walks down to the square at dusk and stands with whoever needs standing with.

options.label: Done.
options.tooltip: Pay Torvald 5 pennies to wake his iron man for the dusk.

nodes.text: 5 pennies. Charcoal, bellows and a week of my sleep. Done?
He will be on the square when the sun goes down. Do not ask him to dance.

options.label: Did you just talk?
options.tooltip: A talking cat. Of course. It is festival day.

nodes.text: A big grey cat with a torn ear is sitting on the bank, watching the pond the way other people watch a door. She turns one eye on you. 'Mrrp. You. You have hands.'

'The cat is Kelda, and the cat talks when there is something worth saying. Here it is. There are cod in this pond. Five, please. Cod, not salmon. Not the little striped ones either: those are a different matter, and not for today. Use the rod. Put them in the dish. The cat will be grateful, in its way.'

options.label: We'll carry Pip up.
options.tooltip: Scoop Pip up in a bucket and carry him to the upper pond.

nodes.text: The cave is green and dripping and lit by glowing berries. Kelda sits by the lower pond beside a small pink axolotl. 'This is Pip. Pip knows fish. All of them. The little striped ones especially, and there are thousands of kinds of those, and the cat... never mind what the cat. Pip wants the upper pond, where the light is. The cat cannot carry a bucket. You can.'

Pip looks up at you and smiles, as axolotls do. 'A friend of hers? Then listen. A Kob, white on red, is not a Kob, red on white. Nobody listens. She listens. Two hundred and eleven kinds she has studied with me, and not one of them muddled.' Kelda looks at the ceiling.
'Of nothing. Of fish. The cat was making conversation.' Kelda washes a paw with great attention. Behind her, Pip blows a bubble that sounds a great deal like a laugh.

options.label: Anywhere else to see?
options.tooltip: Is there anywhere else interesting you could show me?

options.label: Just one more place?
options.tooltip: Just one more place? Anywhere at all?

options.label: You know every corner.
options.tooltip: You know every corner of this town, don't you?

options.label: I'll find you a salmon.
options.tooltip: Please? I'll find you a salmon.

options.label: I'm not leaving.
options.tooltip: I'm not leaving until you show me.

nodes.text: Kelda lies in the sun at the cave mouth with her eyes closed and her tail over her nose. One ear turns toward you.
'The cat has eaten. The cat is going to sleep now. Do not bother the cat.'
'The cat is asleep. This is the cat, asleep. Observe the cat sleeping, quietly, somewhere else.'
'The cat knows every corner of eleven harbours, two mountains and one desert. The cat is not telling. The cat is digesting.'
'A salmon. The cat has had salmon, out of a river that runs uphill, in a country you have never heard of. Do not tempt the cat. The cat is asleep.'
'Mrrrrrow. Fine. There is no getting rid of you, is there. One more place. Keep up, and touch nothing that is not yours. Some of it is very sharp.'
Kelda sits in the corner of the still room beside a bale of dried herbs. She looks at the bale, and then at you, very hard.
Kelda lies curled on her red bed, one eye open. 'The cat's den is the cat's. What is in the chest is yours now. The cat has no more use for it: the cat has retired. Mostly.'

'The stone one? A likeness, and not a good one. The cat has seen the real one, in another town, far gloomier than this: rain every day, and nobody laughed. It got away.' Kelda's whiskers twitch. 'A pity. It would make a delicious grilled octopus.'
